..
Issued at 1242 AM CST Sun Nov 8 2026

The 500 hPa closed low is slowing down as it places all of South 
Texas under abundant diffluence aloft through Monday night as the 
low itself begins to fill. At the surface, a surface boundary has 
set up west of Alice, spanning north to south. This is helping push 
in Gulf moisture into South Texas and setting up an area of moisture 
convergence. At the same time, a low LLJ will start advecting 
additional moisture at the low to mid-levels. We're already seeing 
1.7"+ PWATs advecting into South Texas. Given all these factors, in 
addition to elevated instability and some slantwise/CSI instability, 
we're in for a soggy 24-36 hr period across South Texas. Comparing 
what is being forecast (at least from the ECMWF, the Extreme 
Forecast Index (EFI) for Laredo has been between 0.85 to near 1.0 
with a Shift of Tails (SOT) closer to the 2-4 range for QPF. In 
otherwords, what the model is forecasting is extreme outlook for QPF 
relative to the model climatology while the high SOT is indicating 
that the event will substantially outperform the mean. This is 
further supports the overall trend of a high spread amount global 
and CAM solutions. While these statistical evaluations show the 
potential for the higher end of solutions remaining a possibility, 
this does not lead to the confidence as to 1) where the highest 
rainfall amounts will fall and 2) the magnitude of these amounts. 
While the overall soils will be able to absorb a good portion of the 
forecast rainfall, any moderate to heavy rainfall rates in addition 
to slow-moving storm motion/training will increase the risk for 
flash flooding, especially as these storms move into the more 
urbanized areas across South Texas (such as Laredo, Alice, 
Kingsville, Corpus Christi, etc). There will be several bouts of 
moderate to heavy rainfall (some localized convective storms) 
through the morning and again tonight into Monday morning. In 
between these heavier rounds overall scattered showers will 
continue. The latest forecast is calling for widespread areas of 2-4 
inches along the coastal areas generally from Rockport and locations 
southwest, with the Brush Country seeing greater confidence of 3-6 
inches (accumulations through Monday night). Where convective storms 
move over slowly or train across several bouts will be where higher 
end rainfall amounts of 7-9 inches will be greatest. NBM shows much 
of Webb County under a 20-40% chance of surpassing 6 inches for this 
period. Interestingly, HRRR guidance has been a bit more aggressive 
with an MCS-like structure developing over the Rio Grande Plains 
around 3am and then moving eastward toward the Coastal Bend through 
mid-morning, bringing a localized area of 5-7 inches through this 
afternoon. We will watch this trend carefully especially given the 
urbanized setting in the region.

Isentropically supported showers and storms will start winding 
down Monday night, but rain chances continue Tuesday (20-30% 
chances across South Texas) and Wednesday (20-40% chances along 
the coastal areas and into the Victoria Crossroads). After the 
front clears the area on Thursday, drier air filters into the 
region through Saturday leading to slightly-below to near-normal 
high temperatures. By Sunday, onshore flow returns bringing back 
Gulf moisture into South Texas.

Across our waters, beaches and coastlines, the return of coastal 
flooding concerns begin with the upcoming high tide cycle with P-
ETSS guidance showing water levels reaching 2-2.5 ft above MSL and 
again with Monday's high tide cycle. As such, a Coastal Flood 
Advisory has been issued for Gulf-facing beaches and along the 
bays/estuaries (so if you're an angler hoping to park on the sand 
back along Nueces Bay, you've been warned about the possibility of 
vehicles being cutoff from dry land). Additionally, the easterly 
component of the wind at 20-25 kts will lead to a high rip current 
risk, but will decrease by Monday morning.
